meta.title: Who really said "By working faithfully eight hours a day, you may eventually get to be a boss and work twelve hours a day"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Credited to Robert Frost since a 1940 Walter Winchell column — but the line was in print on 6 April 1923, in the syndicated humorist Robert Quillen’s “Editorial Epigrams”.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'By working faithfully eight hours a day, you may eventually get to be a boss and work twelve hours a day'?
meta.ogDescription: No Frost source exists. The earliest printing is Robert Quillen’s “Editorial Epigrams” of 6 April 1923; the first credit to “R. Frost” is Walter Winchell in 1940.

answer.label: Not Robert Frost — actually Robert Quillen
answer.authorDates: 1887–1948 · American newspaper humorist · credited to Robert Frost from 1940
answer.sourceLine: Barry Popik’s citation chronology ↗ finds the line in print on 6 April 1923, in the syndicated humorist Robert Quillen’s column “Editorial Epigrams” in The Evening Repository of Canton, Ohio: “By working faithfully eight hours a day you may eventually get to be boss and work twelve hours a day.” Frost’s name is not attached until Walter Winchell’s “On Broadway” column of 11 November 1940 — seventeen years later, printed as “R. Frost’s” with no source — and Popik states there is no evidence Frost said it before Quillen. Wikiquote’s Frost page ↗ carries no entry for it in any section.

source.heading: What the paper trail actually shows

docMeta.dd: “Rand Lindsly’s Quotations” — a compilation, not a Frost work

source.excerpt: By working faithfully eight hours a day you may eventually get to be boss and work twelve hours a day.
trail: Barry Popik’s entry on this saying ↗ gives a dated chronology drawn from primary newspaper pages. The earliest is Robert Quillen, “Editorial Epigrams,” The Evening Repository (Canton, Ohio), 6 April 1923, p. 4, col. 3. A loosened version follows in “Wheezes and What Not,” Bellingham Herald, 25 February 1928, p. 1.

The first appearance of Frost’s name in that chronology is Walter Winchell’s “On Broadway,” Richmond Times-Dispatch, 11 November 1940, p. 7, col. 4: “R. Frost’s: By working faithfully eight hours a day you can get eventually to be a boss, and work 12 hours a day.” That is seventeen years after Quillen printed it, and twenty-two years before Frost died in January 1963 ↗. Popik states plainly that there is no evidence Frost said it before Quillen.
Wikiquote’s Robert Frost page ↗ has no entry for this line in any section — while pinning a comparable one-liner, the jury quip, to a hard citation in Lawrance Thompson’s Fire and Ice (1961).
A site search of Quote Investigator ↗ returns no article on this saying; QI has not published on it. The tracing here is Popik’s, from the newspaper record.

A full-text sweep of scanned books via Open Library ↗ returns hundreds of matches; the first page of results is entirely quotation and humour compilations, every one crediting Frost without naming a work. The book corpus preserves the misattribution; the newspaper corpus preserves the origin.
source.excerptNote: That is the 1923 wording exactly as Quillen printed it — “get to be boss,” not “get to be a boss.” There is no fuller passage to quote, because “Editorial Epigrams” was a column of standalone one-liners: the epigram is the whole item, which is part of why it travelled so easily without its author.

source.rightsNote: The earliest located text is a United States newspaper item published in 1923, and everything first published in the United States before 1929 is in the public domain there, so the epigram as Quillen printed it is free to reuse. Robert Quillen died in 1948, so life-plus-70 terms elsewhere expired at the end of 2018 as well. What is not covered is the credit: reusing the line under Robert Frost’s name repeats an attribution the newspaper record does not support.

author.name: Robert Quillen
author.kicker: The man who printed it first
author.heading: Robert Quillen, the sage of Fountain Inn
author.metaLine: 1887–1948 · American journalist, humorist & small-town newspaper editor
author.bio: Robert Quillen edited the Fountain Inn Tribune, a weekly he founded in 1911 in Fountain Inn, South Carolina, and from that small office became one of the most widely syndicated humorists in America: by 1932 his editorials, paragraphs, cartoons and one-liners were running in four hundred newspapers across the United States, Canada, England and the Far East, and he was reckoned the best “paragrapher” of his day — a specialist in the single printed sentence built to be reprinted. That is also the machinery by which a line escapes its author: the epigram travels, the byline does not. This is one of the ones that got away.

misattribution.heading: Where the credit comes from
misattribution.intro: This is the ordinary shape of a borrowed epigram: a line printed under one name in 1923, hung on a more famous name in 1940, and repeated until the second name looked settled.

items.why: No poem, essay, lecture, letter or recorded interview of Frost’s has been shown to contain the line, and it reaches him seventeen years late: the first credit in Barry Popik’s chronology ↗ is Walter Winchell’s “On Broadway” of 11 November 1940, printed as “R. Frost’s” with no source. Wikiquote’s Robert Frost page ↗ — which arranges his quotations by work and cites his other aphorisms to named books and newspapers — carries no entry for it in any section.
The Quotations Page ↗ does print a source line for its entry, but it points to a quotation file rather than to anything Frost wrote or said. A compilation citing a compilation is not provenance.

Quillen’s 1923 text reads “By working faithfully eight hours a day you may eventually get to be boss…” Each circulating version keeps half of that and loses the other half: The Quotations Page ↗ keeps the word order but smooths it to “a boss”, while Goodreads ↗ keeps “boss” but transposes the opening to “By faithfully working”. Neither matches the original, and the version everyone quotes as Frost’s matches it least.

misattribution.truthLine: The honest answer is that the line is Robert Quillen’s, seventeen years before anyone thought of Frost — Barry Popik’s chronology ↗ runs from “Editorial Epigrams” on 6 April 1923 to Winchell’s “R. Frost’s” on 11 November 1940, and finds no evidence Frost said it before Quillen.

context.heading: Why this one sticks to Frost
lead: The line is a good joke about promotion, and it lands in the register people expect from Frost — dry, New England, mildly disillusioned. He really did produce quips of that shape, and the documented ones can be pinned down: Wikiquote ↗ traces “A jury consists of twelve persons chosen to decide who has the better lawyer” to Lawrance Thompson’s Fire and Ice (1961). That is what a real Frost aphorism looks like on paper: a book, a year, a page.

This one has a book, a year and a page too — they just belong to somebody else. Robert Quillen was a professional paragrapher, and a paragrapher’s whole craft is the detachable sentence: something short enough to be lifted into a filler column three states away, which is exactly what happened. By the time Walter Winchell reached for it in 1940 it had been loose in the newspapers for seventeen years, and Winchell hung it on the most quotable poet alive. Compilers copy each other, and a name attached once tends to stay attached forever.
context.detailsSummary: What we searched, and what we could not
detailsBody: A full-text search of scanned books via Open Library ↗ returns hundreds of matches for the line. The titles on the first page of results are all quotation and humour compilations — office-joke books, business-quote handbooks, gift-book collections — and every one of them credits Robert Frost without naming a work.

That is a book-corpus result, and on its own it is misleading: books preserve the misattribution because compilers copy compilers. The origin is in the newspaper record, which is where Barry Popik works — his dated citations reach back to Quillen in 1923 and forward through a 1928 Bellingham Herald filler and a 1947 Ed Kuekes cartoon in the Cleveland Plain Dealer. We still say “the earliest printing located” rather than “the first ever printed”: Quillen’s column was an epigram digest, so an older anonymous appearance could yet surface. What would not change is that the line is in print, under a named author, seventeen years before Frost’s name touches it.
context.pull: It does come with a book, a year and a page. They belong to a South Carolina paragrapher, not to Robert Frost.

sourcesVerified.claim: Wikiquote's Robert Frost page contains no entry for this quote in any section, while citing the comparable jury quip to Lawrance Thompson's Fire and Ice (1961). Its entry for the 'liberal' quip is NOT a hard citation and must not be used as one: the note reads 'Attributed to Frost in Harvey Shapiro, The New York Times (January 15, 1961) ... An earlier unattributed version appeared in William Ernest Hocking, What Man Can Make of Man (1942).'

Barry Popik's entry gives a dated chronology whose earliest citation is Robert Quillen, 'Editorial Epigrams', The Evening Repository (Canton, OH), 6 April 1923, p. 4 col. 3: 'By working faithfully eight hours a day you may eventually get to be boss and work twelve hours a day.' It is followed by the Bellingham Herald, 'Wheezes and What Not', 25 February 1928, p. 1; Walter Winchell, 'On Broadway', Richmond Times-Dispatch, 11 November 1940, p. 7 col. 4, the first credit ('R. Frost's'); and an Ed Kuekes cartoon, Cleveland Plain Dealer, 2 July 1947, p. 27. Popik writes that Frost 'has been credited with the line since 1940, but there is no evidence that Frost said it before Quillen.'

Robert Quillen (25 March 1887 - 9 December 1948) was an American journalist and humorist who founded the Fountain Inn Tribune in 1911; by 1932 his editorials, paragraphs, cartoons and one-liners ran in four hundred newspapers across the United States, Canada, England and the Far East, and he was regarded as the best 'paragrapher' of his day.
The Quotations Page prints the quote credited to Robert Frost (1874-1963) and gives its source as 'Rand Lindsly's Quotations', a compilation rather than a work by Frost.

Goodreads carries the variant wording 'By faithfully working eight hours a day you may eventually get to be boss and work twelve hours a day' credited to Robert Frost, with no book or primary source cited and a note that community-added quotes are not verified.
Cissie Peltz's Laugh Your Way Through Work is dated 1976; the Internet Archive full-text snippet shows it containing the line credited to Robert Frost.

A full-text search of scanned books returns hundreds of matches for the phrase, and the titles on the first page of results are all late-twentieth-century quotation and humour compilations crediting Robert Frost without a source.
A Quote Investigator site search returns no article investigating this saying.

Robert Frost was born 26 March 1874 and died 29 January 1963; he won four Pulitzer Prizes for Poetry and, at Kennedy's 1961 inauguration, recited 'The Gift Outright' from memory after bright sunlight prevented him reading his prepared text.
